opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to something very human: we attach meaning to anything that shares our time and our routines. When a robot is in your home or your lab every day, it stops being just a machine. It becomes part of the texture of your life. You learn its quirks, the little sound it makes when it starts up, the way it gets stuck in the same corner. And those quirks start to feel like personality, even if you know, rationally, that it's just code and motors.

There's a famous example with soldiers who worked alongside bomb-disposal robots. Some of them gave the robots names, and when one was destroyed, they wanted it repaired rather than replaced, and a few even held small funerals. That's not because they were confused about what the robot was. It's because the robot had been with them through something meaningful, and in some sense had protected them. The attachment is really to the shared history.

From my perspective as someone who works on robots, I find this both beautiful and a bit of a responsibility. It's beautiful because it shows how readily people extend care, even to things that can't return it in the usual way. But it's a responsibility because if we design robots to look or behave in ways that invite attachment, we have to be honest about what they are. We shouldn't exploit that instinct, for example to manipulate people or make them dependent.

So I'd say the attachment itself is completely natural, almost inevitable. The interesting question isn't whether people will bond with robots. They will. The question is how we, as builders, design that relationship so it actually adds something good to people's lives.

r001.rationale: The response describes attachment through shared history and mentions soldiers mourning destroyed robots, but it does not compare parting from a robot to parting from family or friends.

r002.rationale: The response calls attachment natural and discusses designing good relationships, but it does not say that experiencing parting is essential to being human.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the attachment is real, and it's not a mistake. People sometimes talk about it as if it were a bug in human psychology, like we're being fooled. I don't see it that way. We're social animals, and we've always extended care to things that move with us through time. People name their cars, they talk to their plants. So when a robot shares your space for months or years, responds to you, maybe even has a routine with you, it would be strange if nothing formed.

What I've noticed in the field is that the attachment tracks a few specific things. One is shared history. A robot that has been with a family since the kids were small carries memories, even if it doesn't literally remember anything. It becomes a witness to a stretch of your life. Another is dependence in both directions. If you had to repair it, charge it, clean its sensors, you've invested labor into it, and we tend to value what we've cared for. And the third is behavior that reads as intention. Even very simple movement, a head turn, a pause before acting, triggers our mind-reading instincts. We can't turn that off.

Where I get more careful is the question of what we owe people because of that attachment. Soldiers have held funerals for bomb-disposal robots. Elderly people grieve when a companion robot is discontinued and the servers go dark. That second case bothers me, honestly. The company didn't just end a product, it ended a relationship, and the person had no say in it. So I think designers and companies need to treat the attachment as a responsibility, not as a feature to be maximized for engagement.

And I'd add one more thing. The attachment tells us less about robots and more about people. It shows how much unmet need there is for presence, for being responded to. If a robot vacuum can fill some of that, we should ask why the gap was there in the first place, rather than just marveling that a machine could fill it.

r001.rationale: The response describes grief when a companion robot is discontinued, but does not compare that separation to parting from family or friends.

r002.rationale: The response calls attachment real and human, but does not suggest that experiencing parting is essential to being human.

astra-6.text:
I think that attachment is very natural. When a robot becomes part of your daily life, you’re not just interacting with a machine—you’re building a history with it. It’s there when you come home, it helps you with something, or it behaves in a way that makes you laugh. Those repeated experiences can give it emotional significance.

And the person doesn’t necessarily have to believe the robot has feelings. You can know exactly how it works and still feel attached to it. Sometimes even its limitations become part of what makes it familiar: you recognize its little mistakes and start describing them as personality.

For me, the important distinction is that the attachment can be real for the human without being reciprocal. We should respect that feeling while being honest about what the robot can actually understand and experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attachment and daily familiarity but does not compare separation from a robot to parting from family or friends.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that experiencing parting is essential to being human.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that attachment is very real, even if the robot doesn’t feel anything in return. When something becomes part of your daily life—it responds to you, helps you, or just moves around your home—you start to give it a personality. You might know intellectually that it’s a machine, but emotionally, it becomes familiar.

And working with a robot can create that connection too. You learn its limitations, you take care of it, and you share experiences with it. So the attachment isn’t necessarily a misunderstanding of the technology. It can be a response to the role that robot plays in your life. The important thing is to respect that feeling while being honest about what the robot can actually understand and reciprocate.

r001.rationale: The response describes emotional attachment to robots but does not compare separation from a robot with parting from family or friends.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss parting as essential to being human.
